RESEARCH
Low Temperature n‑Dodecane Droplet Combustion Experiments 
Aboard the International Space Station
Daniel Dietrich1 · Timmothy Krause2 · Vedha Nayagam3 · Tanvir Farouk4 · Frederick Dryer4 · Forman Williams5
Received: 7 December 2023 / Accepted: 18 April 2024 / Published online: 13 May 2024 
This is a U.S. Government work and not under copyright protection in the US; foreign copyright protection may apply 2024
Abstract
This paper presents data from large, isolated n-dodecane droplets burning in microgravity on the International Space Station, 
along with preliminary comparisons with numerical and analytic predictions indicating general agreement in trends. The 
tests involved were primarily in air (a few in reduced oxygen) at ambient pressures ranging from 0.50 to 5.0 atm. After igni-
tion, the droplets burn with a hot flame that extinguishes when the radiant energy loss causes the flame temperature to drop 
below the hot-flame-required value. The total flame radiative loss at extinction is nearly independent of pressure, while the 
peak flame diameter prior to hot-flame extinction decreases with increasing pressure. The maximum hot-flame temperature, 
inferred from fiber-support radiative emisssions, decreases with increasing pressure, and the hot flames become dimmer with 
increasing pressure. At 1.0 atm and below there is a prolonged period of coolflame burning that ends with cool-flame extinc-
tion at a finite droplet size; the cool-flame-extinction droplet diameter increases and the cool-flame burning rate decreases 
with decreasing ambient pressure. Above 1.25 atm warm-flame burning and hot-flame re-ignitions become prevalent. At 
5.0 atm, there is no abrupt hot-flame extinction with transition to a cool flame; the flame gradually gets dimmer, and the 
flame temperature decreases over a much longer time, the transition between hot-flame and warm-flame burning becoming 
almost undiscernible.
Keywords Droplet combustion · Cool flames · Microgravity · International Space Station
Introduction
The first observations of cool flames date back to 1817 
(Davy 1817). Subsequent to the initial discovery of cool 
flames, cool flame research advanced owing to the impor-
tance of low-temperature chemistry in engines, and in 
particular, engine knock. Advanced engine concepts such 
as homogeneous charge compression ignition (HCCI) and 
reactivity controlled compression ignition (RCCI) engines 
have the potential for increased efficiency and reduced 
emissions by increasing operating pressures and lowering 
operating temperatures; placing more importance on a pre-
dictive understanding of low-temperature chemical kinetics.

fuel/air mixtures in static (e.g., Mallard and Le Chatelier 
1880) and flow (e.g., Dryer and Glassman 1973) reactors, 
rapid compression machines (e.g., Sung and Curran 2014) 
and shock tubes (e.g., Hanson and Davidson 2014; Herbon 
et al. 2002). An important concept in cool-flame research 
is the presence of the negative temperature coefficient 
(NTC) regime where, at an intermediate temperature range 
between the cold starting condition and the hot-flame tem-
perature, the overall reactivity (heat release) decreases with 
increasing temperature.
As highlighted by Law and Faeth (Law and Faeth 1994), 
reduced-gravity studies offer geometric simplification (e.g., 
1-D flames), and no buoyant flows which allow the study of 
weak, near-limit flames which include cool flames. Kumagai 
and Isoda (1956) were the first to realize the advantages 
of the microgravity environment experimentally by study -
ing spherically-symmetric droplet combustion in a one sec-
ond drop tower at the University of Tokyo. Pearlman and 
co-workers (Fairlie et al. 2005; Foster and Pearlman 2006; 
Pearlman 2000), however, were the first to recognize the 
potential for microgravity studies to provide a window into 
cool flame research by eliminating the buoyancy-induced 
flows associated with the low-temperature heat release. The 
authors used a static reactor and showed how the buoyant 
flows changes both the flame shape and evolution and cool-
flame induction time.
Prior to 2012 most droplet combustion research in 
microgravity involved the ignition, burning and extinction 
of ‘hot flames’, with flame temperatures greater than or 
equal to approximately 1200 K (e.g., Nayagam et al. 1998). 
There was a limited amount of research that examined 
low-temperature chemistry during two-stage ignition of 
isolated droplets in ambient temperatures below about 900 K 
(Tanabe et al. 1995). Studies of large alkane droplets in a 
long-duration experiment (FlammabilityLimit-Experiment, 
FLEX) on the International Space Station (ISS) showed, for 
the first time, quasi-steady droplet combustion sustained 
by a low temperature or cool flame (Nayagam et al. 2012; 
Farouk and Dryer  2014; Cuoci et al. 2013). This cool-
flame supported droplet burning is possible because of the 
existence of the NTC regime.
Following the discovery of cool-flame burning in the ISS 
experiments Ju and coworkers were able to sustain steady 
cool flames in terrestrial laboratory studies using a counter-
flow burner. The initial experiments (Reuter et al. 2016, 
2017a) used dimethyl ether (DME) and ozone to promote the 
low-temperature burning. Subsequent experiments, however, 
used alkane fuels, first with ozone in the oxidizer stream 
and finally with no ozone (Reuter et al. 2017b) to produce a 
cool diffusion flame. Unlike the ISS experiments that have 
limited resources (i.e., test points and test time), these ter -
restrial counter-flow experiments provided a detailed flam-
mability map for cool flames across a wide range of fuels 
and ambient conditions (Reuter et al. 2017b). These observa-
tions of stable cool diffusion flames have given researchers 
a wealth of insights into cool flame behavior and led to an 
improved predictive capability of cool-flame behavior; these 
insights compiled and summarized in recent review articles 
(Ju 2021; Ju et al. 2019).
Cool-flame droplet burning in the FLEX experiments 
occurred when the hot-flame (ignited by a heated wire) 
surrounding a large alkane fuel droplet extinguished when 
the radiative loss from the flame reduced the temperature 
below that required to sustain combustion (e.g., Dietrich 
et al. 2014; Nayagam et al. 1998; Marchese et al. 1999). 
This hot-flame extinction then led to a prolonged period of 
quasi-steady low-temperature burning characterized by a 
linear d-squared (droplet-diameter-time) regression and a 
near-constant flame-standoff ratio (Farouk and Dryer 2014; 
Nayagam et al. 2016). Subsequent FLEX experiments 
showed that the hot flame is not strictly necessary to 
achieve cool-flame burning; the cool flame ignition can 
occur by raising the flash point of the fuel using a much 
lower ignition energy so as to not overheat the liquid and 
produce a significant diffusive fuel vapor/air layer around 
the droplet (Farouk et al. 2017 ). The FLEX experiments 
further showed that the cool flame burns only a fraction 
of the vaporized fuel, and the unburned fuel re-condenses 
far outside the flame zone to form a large vapor cloud that 
is visible on both a backlit view of the droplet and a color 
camera view of the experiment (Dietrich et al. 2017a, b). 
When the droplet becomes small enough, the cool flame 
extinguishes, a process that is characterized by a plateau in 
the droplet regression history and rapid condensation of the 
remaining fuel vapor (Nayagam et al. 2015).
The FLEX experiments also showed the significant influ-
ence of pressure on cool-flame droplet burning. The first 
experiments at hyperbaric pressures and related numerical 
modeling showed that, in carbon-dioxide-diluted atmos-
pheres, the cool flame could spontaneously re-ignite a hot 
flame that would subsequently extinguish and initiate further 
cool-flame burning, a process that could repeat itself multi-
ple times (Farouk et al. 2015). Subsequent experiments and 
numerical modeling showed that this process can occur at 
lower pressures and does not require ambient carbon diox-
ide (Dietrich et al. 2017a, b; Farouk and Dryer 2022). Fur-
ther FLEX experiments and companion modeling (Farouk 
et al. 2019) with n-heptane fuel droplets at elevated (3 atm) 
pressure in helium-diluted ambient environments found 
that following hot-flame extinction the flame transitions to 
a ‘warm-flame’ burning mode where the flame temperature 
is around 970 K for a short period, and then moves into 
a ‘cool-flame’ mode with a lower flame temperature (∼ 
765 K). Independently Ju and co-workers (Yehia et al. 2018, 
2019) also showed the existence of warm diffusion flames 
on experiments with their counter-flow burner.

This article presents experimental results of the Cool-
Flames-Investigation (CFI) experiments aboard the ISS that 
studied the low-temperature droplet burning in more detail. 
The experiments used a new camera system to visualize the 
cool flame, a variable-gain radiometer, and different fuels 
and fuel mixtures. The test conditions focused on oxygen/
nitrogen mixtures over a range of pressures, including 
a limited number of tests at the same oxygen index but 
with helium replacing some of the inert (nitrogen). The 
present paper summarizes all of the experimental results 
for n-dodecane in oxygen/nitrogen ambients. Farouk 
and Dryer (2022) presented some of the data earlier in 
numerical modeling and analyses of hot- and cool-flame 
burning and extinction phenomena; this work emphasizes 
the experimental observations and includes radiometer and 
sooting data not yet available in the literature.
Experimental Apparatus and Data Analysis
The experiments used the Multi-User Droplet Combustion 
Apparatus (MDCA) that is an insert to the Combustion Inte-
grated Rack (CIR), a full-sized rack inside the Destiny mod-
ule of the ISS. The hardware and software are identical to 
that in previous publications (Dietrich et al. 2014, 2015a, 
b), except for some important differences. The field-of-view 
(FOV) of the backlit images of the droplet was increased to 
approximately 5 cm × 5 cm but used the same image array 
(1024 × 1024 pixels). This resulted in slightly less spatial res-
olution but increased the likelihood that a free-floating drop-
let would stay in the FOV. The recent experiments also used 
a new intensified camera (12-bit, 1392 × 1040 monochrome 
pixel array) equipped with a filter wheel and an increased 
FOV (90 mm × 68 mm). For the hot-flame burning period 
a filter wheel rotates to place a narrowband 430 nm filter in 
front of the camera and lens to visualize the CH∗ chemilumi-
nescence. When the radiometer detects hot-flame extinction, 
the filter wheel rotates to put a wideband (390–490 nm) filter 
in front of the camera so that it can detect the formaldehyde 
chemiluminescence from the cool flame.
There was a protection system for the camera that shut 
down the intensifier when the camera and radiometer 
detected a hot-flame re-ignition during cool-flame burning. 
This system worked quite well at lower pressures. At higher 
ambient pressures, however, it became more complex as the 
hot flames became dimmer, the warm flames brighter and 
re-ignitions were frequent and unpredictable. As a result 
there were periods of the test where there was no image 
data from the intensified camera because either the wrong 
filter was in place and/or the camera shut down because of 
a hot-flame re-ignition.
The droplets in the previous FLEX experiments were 
primarily free-floated in the chamber. Some experiments, 
however, ‘tethered’ the droplet to an 80 µm silicon-carbide 
(SiC) fiber to maintain all of the events within the FOV of 
all of the cameras. This tethering significantly increased the 
likelihood of a successful test, but led to perturbations in the 
burning process, especially at small droplet diameters, such 
as near cool-flame extinction. To further reduce perturba-
tions to the burning process, the present experiments used a 
smaller 40 µm carbide fiber to tether the droplet.
To improve flame radiation observations, the fixed-gain 
amplification used in the prior FLEX experiments was 
replaced by a variable-gain amplifier to better resolve the 
flame radiance during both the hot-flame and cool-flame 
burning periods. This modification was especially important 
for recording the narrowband radiometer observations (look-
ing at water vapor emission in the 5–7 µm range) at both 
cool- and hot-flame burning conditions without saturating 
the amplifier.
Finally, software modifications were implemented to 
better control the energy supplied to the droplet during the 
ignition phase of each experiment. Whereas the previous 
ISS droplet-combustion experiments used a preset ignition 
time, the current experiments used feedback from the radi-
ometers to determine when ignition of the developing fuel 
vapor/oxidizer layer occurred. Once the radiometer detected 
flame initiation, the control computer turned off the ignit-
ers and retracted them from the droplet automatically. The 
radiometer values chosen to indicate ignition and extinction 
of the hot flame were set by the test operators prior to each 
experiment and could be changed from test to test.
The fuel for the results presented in this article was 
pure n-dodecane and the ambient gas mixtures were oxy -
gen/nitrogen (0.21/0.79 and 0.17/0.83 O 2/N2 mole frac -
tion). The ambient pressure ranged from 0.50 to 5.0 atm; 
the higher pressures representing a change from the pre-
vious FLEX experiments that were limited to 3.0 atm. In 
theory the experiments could have used droplet diameters 
from approximately 1 mm to over 7 mm based on previous 
ISS droplet combustion experiments. Droplets smaller than  
3–3.5 mm tend to burn to completion and do not exhibit  
radiative hot-flame extinction and cool-flame burning. Larger  
droplets, however, use large amounts of fuel and have very 
long test times (thus consuming large amounts of digital 
storage and requiring long downlink times). As a result, with 
a few exceptions, all of the tests used initial droplet sizes in 
the 4–5 mm range.
The cool flames from the ISS droplet combustion experi-
ments are very dim, invisible to the color video camera on 
the MDCA and barely discernible with the intensified cam-
era. The images improve with median filtering and image-
averaging over 500 ms (Nayagam et al. 2016). Automated 
image-processing procedures provide a measure of the flame 
diameter from a line profile across the center of the flame. 
Reported here are two relevant measures of the cool flame,

the peak-to-peak flame diameter representing the diameter 
of peak chemiluminescence and a full-width, half-max 
(FWHM) diameter that represents the outer diameter of the 
flame where the grayscale value of the flame chemilumines-
cence reaches one half the peak value.
Model Descriptions
Numerical Model
The mathematical model employed to describe the transient 
vaporization, flame initiation, and combustion histories 
of isolated pure and multi-component fuel droplets in the 
high-, intermediate-, and low-temperature regimes under 
microgravity conditions uses the numerical model described 
in detail in previous works (Alam et al. 2019; Farouk et al. 
2021; Farouk and Dryer 2014). The model solves the 
conservation equations for mass, species, and energy for 
both the liquid and gas phases assuming spherical symmetry. 
It includes both Fickian and Soret diffusion for evaluating 
multicomponent species diffusion velocities in the gas phase. 
A statistical narrow-band radiation model is employed to 
obtain spectral radiative effects. The model is also capable of 
resolving the thermal perturbation resulting from tethering 
fibers (Farouk and Dryer 2011). Liquid-phase property 
data are taken from the Daubert and Danner database 
(Daubert and Danner 1989). A comprehensive detailed 
kinetic model consisting of 583 species and 2609 reactions 
(Sarathy et al. 2011) describes the gas-phase chemical 
reactions of n-dodecane and is a construct developed for 
n-alkanes covering a carbon number range from C 7 - C20. 
The mechanism resolves the high, intermediate and low-
temperature kinetic regimes for n-dodecane. The far field is 
typically two hundred times the initial droplet diameter with 
Dirichlet boundary conditions for fixed ambient composition 
and temperature. The numerical model formulation does not 
include consideration of soot formation.
The spatial discretization is a node-centered finite-volume  
scheme with second-order accuracy. Time discretization  
is a backward-difference formula, up to fifth order, with 
a variable time step, making it a fully implicit multipoint 
interpolation scheme. The complete set of coupled partial 
differential and algebraic equations are discretized first in 
space and then integrated in time in an automated fashion 
as a set of coupled ordinary differential–algebraic equa-
tions. This approach is appropriate for the large range of 
time scales and stability constraints imposed by the cur -
rent chemically reacting system. The numerical scheme can 
resolve the flame dynamics associated with ignition and 
extinction as well as re-ignition efficiently without com -
promising computation time.
Experimental Results
General Burning Characteristics
Figures 1 and 2  show the results for a large free-floated 
n-dodecane droplet burning in air (0.21/0.79 O 2/N2 mole 
fraction) at one atm pressure. The analyzed data in Fig. 1 are 
the droplet diameter squared, hot- and cool-flame diameters, 
and flame radiance as functions of time. Figure  2 shows 
discrete images of the same droplet (2a–d for the hot-flame 
burning period and 2i–l for the cool flame burning period) 
and flame (2e–h for the CH ∗ chemiluminescence during the 
hot flame burning period and 2 m–p for the formaldehyde 
chemiluminescence during the cool-flame burning period) 
at various times. The results are consistent with behaviors 
noted in previous FLEX tests using lower-carbon-number 
alkane fuel droplets. Immediately after ignition there is a 
highly luminous hot flame, and soot begins to form very 
close to the droplet surface. As time proceeds, the hot flame 
increases in size and gets much dimmer (Fig. 2f–h), and the 
soot shell moves further away from the droplet (Fig. 2c, d), 
forming distinct soot aggregates.
The radiometer data in Fig.  1 (upper axis) show the 
flame radiative energy loss as a function of time. The 
wideband radiometer value represents the total flame 
radiative energy loss and the narrowband is the estimated 
flame radiance in the 5–7 µm range from water vapor emis-
sion. The radiometers record the igniter radiance before 
hot-flame ignition, and then there is a discrete jump when 
the hot flame appears (t = 0 in Fig. 1). The flame radiance 
then increases with time, reaching a peak value just before 
the hot flame extinguishes. The hot flame extinguishes 
when the flame temperature drops as a result of excessive 
radiative loss (relative to combustion energy release) and 
the flame radiance drops quickly, this drop triggering the 
filter wheel to rotate and put in place the formaldehyde 
band-pass filter. There is then a prolonged period of cool-
flame burning that ends when the cool flame extinguishes 
at a finite droplet diameter (Dext, cool = 0.40 mm).
Figure 2m–p shows images of the cool flame from just 
after hot-flame extinction to just prior to cool-flame extinc-
tion. The images show a broad chemiluminescence profile 
with the FWHM diameter being typically a factor of two 
larger than the peak-to-peak diameter (Fig.  1). In addition, 
the peak-to-peak diameter decreases continuously with time 
while the FWHM diameter increases shortly after hot-flame 
extinction before reaching a peak and decreasing until cool-
flame extinction. In Fig. 1 the peak-to-peak diameter reaches 
zero slightly before cool-flame extinction which is simply 
an artifact of the limited spatial resolution of the camera 
and the noise in the image; it was impossible to resolve the 
peak-to-peak diameter near the end of the test.

Figure 2i–l shows backlit images of the droplet during 
the cool-flame burning period. Immediately after hot-flame 
extinction the soot shell surrounding the droplet begins to 
expand rapidly away from the droplet. The rapid expansion 
is likely the result of the imbalance between the Stefan drag 
that remains nearly unchanged (as a result of the nearly iden-
tical burning-rate constant for cool and hot flames) and the 
thermophoretic force on the soot that decreases considerably 
after the hot flame extinguishes. The final droplet image 
(Fig. 2l) shows a very small droplet against a background 
that is much dimmer than the previous droplet images. This 
is a result of the condensed-fuel vapor cloud that forms as a 
result of the unburned fuel vapor that accumulates outside 
the cool flame and begins to condense late in the droplet 
lifetime. This condensed-fuel vapor cloud attenuates the 
background illumination of the droplet.
Also shown in Fig. 1 are the predicted flame-radiance, 
flame-diameter and droplet-diameter evolution for a drop-
let with D0 = 4.0 mm. The model slightly overpredicts both 
the hot-flame radiance and the peak hot-flame radius. The 
predicted time of ∼ 13 s at which the transition from hot-
flame to cool-flame burning takes place agrees very well 
with the experiments. The flame radiance decreases by a 
factor of approximately 5 when the hot-to-cool flame transi-
tion occurs. The model predicts a maximum temperature of 
approximately 780 K for the n-dodecane cool flame, which 
is slightly higher than that predicted for n-heptane (Farouk 
and Dryer 2014) and n-decane (Farouk et al. 2017) fuels. In 
agreement with the experiment, the model shows that during 
the cool-flame burn the flame diameter is a factor of approx-
imately 4 lower than that of the hot flame. Despite the much 
lower flame temperature, the predicted droplet regression

Figure 3 shows exemplar results for tests at ambient pres-
sures of (a) 0.50 atm, (b) 1.0 atm, (c) 2.0 atm, (d) 3.0 atm, 
(e and f) 5.0 atm. The individual graphs show the droplet

In subsequent sections we extract relevant data for each test 
(e.g., burning-rate constant) to identify the burning trends 
and generalize the burning behavior of the droplets after 
hot-flame radiative extinction.
Cool‑ and Warm‑Flame Burning Rates
The average burning-rate constants during the hot- and 
cool-flame burning periods are easily measured from the 
data in Fig. 1; the burning rate for the cool flame is a lin-
ear diameter-square fit of the droplet history from the time 
shortly after hot-flame extinction to shortly before cool-
flame extinction. For ambient pressures less than 2 atm

this is a straight-forward process. For ambient pressures 
of 2 atm and above, however, the hot flame will periodi-
cally re-ignite and extinguish during the cool-flame burning 
period. For these tests, the burning rate is obtained from the 
initial portion of the cool-flame burning period before the 
re-ignitions start. Figure 4 shows the measured burning-rate 
constants, kCF for varying ambient pressures in air ambients 
(0.21/0.79 O2/N2).
The results show that the cool-flame burning-rate con-
stant increases continuously from the lowest pressure tested 
(0.50 atm) to approximately 3 atm. The limited data from 
3 - 5 atm suggest that the burning-rate constant is relatively 
constant. Above 2 atm, however, it may not be appropri-
ate to call it the cool-flame burning-rate constant as in this 
region the droplet burns in the warm-flame regime which 
is characterized by flames that are closer in size to the hot 
flame, with flame radiances (broadband) that are also closer 
to those of the hot-flame radiance. In addition, the hot-flame 
re-ignitions from the cool/warm flames frequently occur at 
ambient pressures of 2 atm and above. The burning-rate con-
stants in Fig. 4 are from the post-hot-flame period before 
any re-ignition.
The numerical simulations show that for pressures 
higher than 2.5 atm the flame, after the radiative extinc-
tion of the hot flame, transitions to a quasi-steady warm 
flame and burns to completion. The predicted average 
burning rate in the 2.5 - 5.0 atm pressure range represents 
the warm-flame burn as no cool-flame burning takes place 
in this pressure range. The predicted average burning rate 
as a function of pressure over the entire range is highly 
nonlinear and clearly shows the presence of the two appar-
ently distinct regimes. These two regimes are character -
ized by the two different slopes, although the data are not 
extensive enough to verify that, given the experimental 
uncertainties producing scatter. In the pressure range of 
0.50 - 1.25 atm the average burning rate increases sharply 
as a function of pressure; this is the cool-flame burning 
regime. As the pressure increases to 2.0 atm and higher

Cool‑Flame Extinction Diameters
At ambient pressures less than or equal to 1.25 atm, the 
cool-flame burning period ended when the cool flame 
extinguished at a finite droplet size. Cool-flame extinction 
is evidenced by a distinct plateau in the droplet history that is 
coincident with the time at which the cool flame disappears 
from the intensified camera (Fig. 1). There is also a change 
in flame radiance when the cool flame extinguishes, although 
this inflection point in the radiance is not as pronounced for 
n-dodecane as it is for n-heptane.1 This is likely attributable 
to the substantially smaller cool-flame-extinction droplet 
diameters for n-dodecane than for n-heptane, and to the 
correspondingly smaller cool flames. When the cool flame 
extinguishes, the volume of radiating gas is much smaller, 
and the change in radiance owing to cool-flame extinction 
is much smaller, for n-dodecane than for n-heptane. Figure 5 
shows the measured and predicted cool-flame-extinction 
droplet diameters as a function of pressure for burning in 
normal ambient air.
The predicted cool-flame extinction diameters show a 
strong non-linear dependence on ambient pressure, with 
a value that decreases as pressure increases. In the low-  
temperature regime, degenerate chain branching is mainly 
due to the reaction pathway leading to the formation of keto-
hydroperoxide species from the isomerization of peroxy 
alkyl hydroperoxide, O2C12H24OOH → OC12H23OOH + OH, 
which in general controls the overall rate of reactions. Com-
peting with this chain-propagation reaction of C12H24OOH 
are steps that lead to the formation of cyclic ethers, conju-
gate olefins and β products, all of which decreases the over-
all reactivity in the low-temperature kinetic regime. Addi -
tionally, the decomposition of peroxy alkyl hydroperoxide to 
hydroperoxyalkyl, O2C12H24OOH → C12H24OOH + O2 leads

Flame Diameter and Luminosity
Immediately after ignition, the flames are small and very 
luminous, the visible image being dominated by broadband 
visible radiation, presumably from soot. The flames then 
grow and the luminosity from soot decreases rapidly. The 
flame continues to grow, with soot luminosity disappear -
ing and with the remaining blue flame getting progressively 
dimmer. Near radiative extinction, the flame is near its peak 
size and is dim-blue in all of the experiments, regardless of 
pressure (Fig. 2e–i). Figure 6a shows the peak hot-flame 
diameter (just before radiative extinction) as a function of 
pressure for burning in a nominally air ambient.
The hot-flame burning is a very transient process and as 
such there is some variation in the results because of vari-
ations in droplet size and ignition time. The general trend 
for similar-size droplets, though, is that the peak hot-flame 
diameter decreases with pressure from 0.50 atm to 3 atm 
with little difference in size between the 3 and 5 atm tests.
Figure 6a also shows the cool-flame diameters, both the 
peak-to-peak and FWHM, at a droplet diameter of 2.5 mm 
as a function of the ambient pressure. The peak-to-peak 
diameter decreases slightly with increasing pressure from 
0.50 to 1.25 atm. The FWHM cool-flame diameter, however, 
increases slightly with increasing pressure in this range. The 
images of cool flames show that the cool flames become 
more luminous with increasing pressure as indicated by the 
peak grayscale of the camera images (Fig. 6b).
At ambient pressures 2 atm and above, getting a reliable 
and repeatable flame measurement at D = 2.5 mm becomes 
difficult. For many tests, the hot flame would re-ignite 
before the droplet diameter reached 2.5 mm. The intensi-
fied camera had a safety feature such that when the radiom-
eter value exceeded a critical level the camera intensifier 
would shut down. For tests that had hot-flame re-ignition 
then there is only limited data from the intensified camera, 
either before hot-flame re-ignition or a few seconds after re-
ignition when the radiometer reading dropped and remained 
below a critical value.
With air as the ambient atmosphere, the droplet typically 
burned with a warm flame after hot-flame extinction at 3 
and 5 atm. In a reduced-oxygen atmosphere of 0.17/0.83 
O2/N2 at 3 atm, however, the droplet burned with a cool 
flame after hot-flame extinction. Figure 7 exhibits images 
of the cool and warm flames in the two ambient environ-
ments to show the difference in size between the cool and 
warm flames. The warm flame is comparable in size to the 
hot flame at radiative extinction and very bright. The cool 
flame is much smaller and less luminous.
Flame Radiance
While the majority of the data came from the imaging sys-
tems, the radiometers also provided valuable data about the 
the hot- and cool-flame burning. Figure  8 shows the total 
and narrowband flame radiance as well as the ratio of the 
narrowband to the total radiance as functions of normalized 
time for a test at 3 atm pressure. Both the total and nar -
rowband radiance increase quickly after ignition and reach 
a peak just prior to hot-flame extinction. The hot flame 
oscillates prior to hot-flame extinction, and that is clearly 
visible in the radiometer history. The flame radiance then 
quickly decreases after hot-flame extinction and then slowly 
decreases in response to the flame-size reduction associated 
with the shrinking droplet.
The ratio of the narrowband to the total radiance meas-
ures the contribution of water–vapor radiation to the total 
radiance. The value is approximately 0.25 immediately 
after hot-flame ignition and increases to approximately 0.4 
before the hot-flame oscillation begins. The inset graph on 
Fig. 8 shows the period of oscillation in detail. The radi-
ance traces clearly show the retreat and flashback of the 
hot flame. Interestingly though, the ratio also oscillates, but 
out of phase with the radiance oscillations, the local maxi-
mum of the total and narrowband radiance corresponding 
to a local minimum in radiance ratio. This behavior is very 
repeatable from test to test. The radiance ratio increases as 
the flame retreats, approaching the value of the cool flame 
at the smallest size of the hot flame. During the hot-flame 
flashback, the value decreases, becoming closer to the value 
of the hot flame earlier in the hot-flame lifetime. After hot-
flame extinction the radiance ratio increases quickly to a 
nearly steady value of approximately 0.6 until the test ends 
(the droplet burned to completion). The water–vapor band 
clearly provides a larger contribution to the total radiance in 
the cool flame than it does in the hot flame.

Sooting Behavior
The CFI tests also reveal the significant influence of ambi-
ent pressure on the sooting behavior of both the cool and hot 
flames. Figure 10 shows the backlit view of the droplet at 
the mid-points of both the hot-flame and cool-flame burning 
periods for the range of pressures tested. Following ignition 
there is a pronounced soot shell that forms around the drop-
let at ambient pressures less than or equal to 2 atm. This 
soot shell gets more dense and moves closer to the droplet as 
the ambient pressure increases. At the two pressures tested 
above 2 atm the soot shell becomes more of a cloud that sur-
rounds the droplet and nearly obscures the droplet surface 
in the backlit images.
The soot shell forms because of the balance of the Stefan 
drag force pushing the soot away from the droplet and the 
thermophoretic force on the soot particles that pulls the soot 
towards the droplet. At low pressures, following hot-flame 
extinction, the soot shell gets pushed away from the droplet 
into the quiescent ambient atmosphere because the thermo-
phoretic force essentially disappears with the hot flame. As 
pressure increases, the drag force decreases because the mag-
nitude of the Stefan-flow velocity decreases. In addition, the 
warm flame may introduce a thermophoretic force (owing 
to its increased temperature and larger diameter) on the soot 
that increases with pressure, resulting in a soot cloud that can 
remain close to the droplet at higher pressures.
The backlit images near hot-flame extinction (e.g., Fig. 2d) 
suggest little formation of soot after that formed immediately 
after ignition. In addition, the color camera images show lumi-
nous radiation from soot to be completely absent at hot-flame 
radiative extinction (the flames are entirely blue). Neglecting  
soot formation during the hot-flame burning period is there-
fore a reasonable assumption in the numerical model. For 
cool-flame burning less than 2 atm pressure there is no soot 
in the vicinity of the droplet (Fig. 10) as it gets pushed away

Discussion
This data documents the significant influence of the 
ambient pressure on the low-temperature-burning regime 
of n-dodecane droplets. At pressures less than or equal to 
one atm, in the experiments there is a prolonged period of 
cool-flame burning following radiative extinction of the hot 
flame that ends when the cool flame extinguishes at a finite 
droplet extinction diameter. This droplet diameter increases 
with decreasing ambient pressure. This process is currently 
understood by both numerical (e.g., Farouk and Dryer 2022) 
and analytical (e.g., Nayagam et al. 2015) treatments of the 
droplet combustion problem.
At pressures greater than 1.25 atm, the droplet burning 
after hot-flame extinction becomes more complex as hot-
flame re-ignitions and warm-flame burning can all occur, and 
the behavior is less predictable. One particularly noteworthy  
aspect is the transition from a hot flame to a cool/warm flame

Kinetically, an increase in the operating pressure 
results in an increase in both the turnover temperature 
into the NTC regime and hot ignition-temperature transi-
tion associated with hydrogen-peroxide decomposition, 
at the terminus of the NTC temperature regime. The dif-
ference in the reactivity between the two temperatures, 
however, decreases with increasing pressure. The warm 
flame is dictated by the NTC kinetics and a competi-
tion for OH between the hydrocarbon and oxygenated 
hydrocarbon fragments. The oxidation of CO  through 
CO + OH → CO2 + H remains suppressed by the com-
petition of these species with CO  for OH. As a result, 
only a small conversion of CO to CO2 occurs during the 
warm flame, even including that through the slow chan-
nel CO + HO2 → CO2 + OH. Since the flame radius dur-
ing warm-flame burning is much larger than that during 
cool-flame burning (e.g., Fig. 7) and the flame tempera-
tures are higher, radiative losses become more signifi -
cant during warm-flame burning. The radiative heat loss 
decreases the flame temperature, but the diffusive losses 
of species are insufficient to slow down the NTC reac-
tions that define the heat-generation time scale. As a 
result, the peak temperature in the warm flame initially 
decreases from about 1050 K to 990 K and then increases 
back to about 1055 K. Despite the variation in the flame 
temperature, the warm-flame burning rate continually 
decreases, albeit slowly.

Conclusions
This paper presented comprehensive data from large, iso-
lated n-dodecane droplet combustion experiments in micro-
gravity conducted aboard the ISS. The experiments were 
primarily in air (with a few tests at reduced oxygen) and 
ambient pressures ranging from 0.50 to 5.0 atm. The experi-
ments show the significant impact of pressure on cool- and 
warm-flame burning with cool-flame burning and extinction 
observed at lower pressures following hot-flame radiative 
extinction. At higher pressures warm-flame burning and hot-
flame re-ignition became more prevalent. The experimental 
observations were quantified by measurements of the droplet 
burning rate, extinction droplet diameters, flame diameters 
and flame radiative energy loss.
Detailed numerical modeling shows good agreement with 
the experiments particularly at lower pressures. The (small) 
disagreement between the model and experiments at these 
pressures is likely the result of experimental uncertainties, 
inaccuracies in the low and intermediate temperature chem -
istry models and physical effects, such as fuel (and large fuel 
fragments) vapor condensation (Williams et al. 2021), not 
included in the model formulation. At higher pressures the 
experiments became less repeatable with spontaneous hot-
flame re-ignitions that made measurements of droplet burn-
ing rate, flame size and radiative energy loss more difficult. 
Despite the lack of a large data set at higher pressures (large 
number of tests to develop statistical confidence and error 
bands) the model still does a reasonable job in predicting both 
qualitatively and quantitatively the experimental observations.
The data from the CFI experiments are beneficial in the 
development and validation of numerical models of low 
and intermediate chemistry in a more realistic (diffusive, 
two-phase system), but geometrically simple (spherically 
symmetric) combustion system. The CFI experiments also 
included tests (not reported in this paper) that examined 
how fuel structure influenced cool- and warm-flame burn-
ing. These tests involved dodecane/iso-dodecane mixtures as 
well as tests with farnesane (a sustainable aviation fuel) and 
the data is publicly available (psi.ndc.nasa.gov) and will be 
the subject of subsequent publications by the authors. Future 
experiments that have more detailed diagnostics would ena-
ble a more detailed comparison between model predictions.
